newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Strong Irish growth to last into next decade - ESRI.
newsitem.headline: Strong Irish growth to last into next decade - ESRI.

text.p: Ireland's exceptional economic growth rate is likely to continue into the next decade, helping Irish living standards converge towards the EU average by 2005, a leading economic institute said on Wednesday.

Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) said it expects GNP growth to average 5.5 percent a year in the second half of the 1990s, falling to five percent a year in the period 2000-2005.

"This implies that Ireland will approach the EU average standard of living around the middle of the next decade, probably exceeding that of the UK before 2005," the ESRI said in a medium-term review of the Irish economy.

The Irish economy has outperformed its EU neighbours in recent years, helped by a number of factors such as a changing demographic structure, an increase in human capital, the openness of the economy, investment in infrastructure and the domestic macroeconomic environment, the review said.
The combined effects of an educational revolution and demographic change should continue to exert a major positive influence on developments in the Irish economy through the next decade, it added.
Strong employment growth should lead to a substantial reduction in the jobless rate which the ESRI sees at around 8.6 percent by 2000 and at seven percent by 2005.
With prudent management of the public finances, it should be possible to eliminate all new government borrowing in the next three years and even to run a small surplus by 2005, the ESRI says.
This would be sufficient to reduce Ireland's debt to GNP ratio to around 30 percent by the end of the next decade.
The institute said its forecasts were based on the assumption of prudent fiscal policy, wage moderation and the absence of serious domestic or international shocks.

"The biggest danger domestically is that an excessive rise in expectations could feed into wage inflation or unsupportable demands on the exchequer. This would choke off the rapid growth at a premature stage," the review said.

A lack of investment in physical infrastructure could lead to rising congestion, also damaging the growth potential of the economy while another possible threat would be an inappropriate EU response to the need to halt the global warming process, the ESRI said.
The institute also said there could be an adverse impact on the Irish economy if European economic and monetary union (EMU) failed to go ahead.

"Given the economic and political capital invested in it at an EU level, there would probably be serious disruption of the EU economy, reflected in a substantial rise in interest rates in countries such as Ireland," the ESRI said.
It said Ireland faced a period of up to 20 years of low dependency which would provide a "demographic dividend."
But it warned that this would not last indefinitely and should be reinvested to provide for long-term needs.
"In planning the public finances in the medium term, it is wise to provide for the elimination of new government borrowing to ensure a sustained reduction in our indebtedness," the ESRI said.
This would enhance the scope for future governments to deal with rising pension and dependency burdens, it said.
